catalog_quote: 2.3 PHONEMIC TONE. Foodo has two contrastive tones: high (H) and low (L). The clearest contrast between these two tones occurs in verbs, as shown in example (3). ... /wù/ see ... /wú/ die ... TBUs include the 18 contrastive vowels and the two syllabic nasals ... In addition to the two level tones of H and L, non-automatic downstep occurs in surface forms. This is due to the presence of a L in the tonal melody that is not associated with a TBU. Phonetically, Foodo also has two falling contour tones, one falling to a low and another falling to a downstepped high. ... Therefore, it is preferable to analyze these contour tones as a combination of low and high tones in the tonal melody associated with one TBU. ... audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: every clause of the deciding quotation is present verbatim in the JWAL text we hold at sec. 2.3 (printed p.112) and sec. 1.6 (p.111), as the locator states; 'stress' occurs 0 times in the article. (2) Deciding source: a 2009 peer-reviewed grammar sketch by the language's principal describer; Foodo (North Guang, Kwa) is described as a two-tone (H, L) language with non-automatic and automatic downstep and lexical tonal melodies on nouns and verbs; nothing in the Glottolog bibliography (5 descriptive refs, two of which are mis-assigned English-intonation papers) or in Plunkett's own reference list is a stress/accent study, and the one larger prosodic work (Plunkett 1991, 221 pp) is a tone thesis whose abstract posits two underlying tones. (3) list of works to obtain: Plunkett 1991 is open at UND Scholarly Commons but an automated-access block refused scripted download; record page

sources.citation: Plunkett, Gray C. 1991. The tone system of Foodo nouns. MA thesis, University of North Dakota (Theses and Dissertations 5066). Record page only; PDF blocked by an automated-access block (not reachable by automated download) by automated download and direct download.
sources.access_detail: a digital copy (available on request); access check: open copy online
sources.quote: Abstract: 'This thesis presents an autosegmental analysis of the tone system of the nouns of Foodo, a Guang language of Benin. The goal is to give an analysis of the tone system of nouns that will account for all the surface tonal phenomena by positing two underlying tones.' ... 'This chapter also discusses the issue of what constitutes a tone-bearing unit (TBU) in the language'. No mention of stress or accent in the abstract; full text not obtained.
sources.note: The only book-length treatment of Foodo prosody (221 pp on noun tone, TBU discussion in ch. 6) by the same author as our deciding 32-pp sketch; would let the record cite the primary tone monograph and check for any remark on stress/accent or syllable prominence that the sketch omits.

sources.note: Plunkett 2009 p. 132, after the tonal verb classes, the floating-L imperative/jussive and the H-spreading stative: 'Time does not permit a fuller discussion of the verb system. As these examples show, grammatical tone plays a significant role in the Foodo verb phrase. I refer the compiler to Idrissou Seriki (1993) for a fuller discussion.' The thesis is thus the referred-to fuller description of the verb system; whether it analyses the verbal tone itself is unverified (Glottolog keywords: grm, tam).
